questions.q: What is Brightfield Outfitters, as presented in this lesson?
options: A fictional company invented for this course's illustrative case study, not a real organization or incident
A real retailer named in a regulatory filing
An anonymized real company from a published news report
A subsidiary of Harrow Peak Financial from Lesson 28
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly labels Brightfield Outfitters as fictional and illustrative, unrelated to Lesson 28's separate fictional company.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say this case study's governance problem is fundamentally different from Lesson 28's credit model?
options: A generative chatbot produces open-ended language that can't be exhaustively tested in advance, unlike a model with a small fixed set of outputs
Because chatbots are never risk-tiered
Because generative AI has no documentation requirements at all
Because customer-facing systems are always lower risk than internal ones
questions.explain: The lesson's core distinction is that open-ended generative output can't be pre-certified the way a fixed-output scoring model can.

questions.q: What did Brightfield's model card state before launch, according to the lesson?
options: That the chatbot can produce fluent, confident-sounding answers that are factually wrong about specific order details
That the chatbot has never made an error since launch
That the chatbot is directly connected to every backend database with perfect accuracy
That the chatbot requires no further monitoring once launched
questions.explain: The model card documented this known hallucination-style limitation before launch, per Lesson 12's model-card practice.

questions.q: How did the team score the chatbot's risk tier compared to Harrow Peak's credit model, and why?
options: Lower overall, since impact was more recoverable, but still high enough to require active monitoring rather than a launch-and-forget approach
Identical in every respect to the credit model's risk tier
Zero risk, since chatbots can never cause real harm
Higher than the credit model, because chatbots are always riskier than scoring models
questions.explain: The lesson describes the chatbot's tier as lower than the credit model's (more recoverable impact) but still requiring active monitoring.

questions.q: What happened when the chatbot stated an incorrect return-window policy, per the lesson?
options: The incident-response process triaged it, patched the specific prompt pattern, corrected affected customers, and logged it into the model's documentation
The company ignored the issue since no law required a response
The chatbot was never used again and the company abandoned generative AI entirely
The incident was deleted from all records to avoid embarrassment
questions.explain: The lesson walks through Lesson 22's incident-response process being applied, with the issue logged rather than minimized.
